item.title: Our education must move beyond grades
item.description:
We understand the immediate concern that comes from the drastic decline in this year’s Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examination pass rate.
Dropping by 6.71% down to 52.12%, alongside hundreds of thousands of failures, and institutions recording zero pass rates will inevitably trigger panicked headlines across the country. This newspaper has been no different.
On the surface, such a significant drop cannot simply be brushed aside as an administrative quirk. It is only natural to wonder what has happened for the number of students securing a GPA-5 to fall from 145,911 in 2024 to 40,084 in 2026 -- a drop of more than 72%.
Yet, reacting with reflexive hand-wringing or frantic attempts to massage the numbers misses the deeper, more vital reality.
For decades, our education system has prioritized pass rates and inflated GPA-5 tallies, fostering a culture of rote memorization, coaching-centre dependency, and superficial evaluation that has left our students fundamentally unequipped for the real world.
When students emerge from 12 years of schooling unable to analyze, adapt, or compete in a modernizing global economy, chasing a GPA-5 becomes a hollow and deceptive pursuit.
The state, educators, and parents must stop treating board exams as a bureaucratic obstacle course and start interrogating the structural "whys" behind our chronic learning deficits -- including acute teacher shortages, outdated curricula, and an assessment system that penalizes analytical thought.
Tackling our education crisis requires the government to look beyond annual statistical fluctuations. We need an overhaul of our education culture, one that pivots away from rote memorization toward competency-based education.
A 52% pass rate is a harsh wake-up call, but it should not be treated as a disaster to be masked by artificial grading leniency. Instead, it must serve as the catalyst to dismantle prioritizing grades over all.
It is time to stop chasing cosmetic metrics and finally invest in our youth's future by having an education system that builds capable, well-rounded citizens equipped to excel in life.

item.title: Restoring peace to the hills
item.description:
The recurring clashes and exchanges of gunfire between rival armed groups in Sajek potentially signal a resurgence of instability in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) that must not be taken lightly.
We should not be tolerating territorial rivalries erupting into open gunbattles as innocent local residents are forced to live in constant terror. This is equally true for tourism, local economies, and public safety which are repeatedly held hostage.
Such lawlessness cannot be treated as an inevitable feature of the region; bringing lasting peace, security, and the rule of law to the hills must become an immediate, non-negotiable priority.
For far too long, armed factions in the CHT have continued to operate, waging turf wars for political dominance. All the while, it has been civilian populations that have been affected.
Recent blockades, attacks on tourist convoys, and armed standoffs not only imperil local livelihoods but also directly challenge state authority. Law enforcement and security personnel stating that they struggle to access remote clash sites while communities are caught in the crossfire is simply not enough of a reason.
Peace in the CHT cannot be sustained through temporary ceasefires or passive monitoring from a distance. While political dialogue, genuine socio-economic development, and the full implementation of structural commitments remain vital for long-term reconciliation, the immediate priority must also be to ensure the safety and security of those who call the region home.
The people of the Chittagong Hill Tracts deserve safety, dignity, and economic progress, not perpetual warfare. It is time for the government to commit to the region, first by restoring peace.

item.title: Lack of ICU at National Eye Hospital delays surgery for heart patients
item.description:
Mustafa Kamal, a man in his 60s from Shikarpur village in Uzirpur upazila of Barisal, travelled to the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital in Dhaka for treatment of an eye condition. Following a series of tests, doctors diagnosed a tumour in his eye socket (orbit) and recommended surgery.
However, his history of heart disease complicated the procedure. Doctors said he might require intensive monitoring after surgery. But the hospital, one of the country's leading specialised public eye care facilities, does not have an intensive care unit (ICU). As a result, he was advised to undergo the operation at another hospital.
Kamal said his surgery was initially scheduled at the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital. However, the absence of ICU facilities meant the procedure could not be performed there.
He was advised to seek treatment at another medical college hospital. He subsequently contacted Dhaka Medical College Hospital, Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital and Mugda Medical College Hospital but failed to secure an operation date.
After visiting several hospitals over a number of days, he was told by Dhaka Medical College Hospital that he would have to wait nearly two months for surgery.
Kamal said he had met another heart patient while seeking treatment at the eye hospital. Unable to undergo surgery there, the patient eventually had the procedure at a private hospital.
Kamal said he had met another heart patient while seeking treatment at the eye hospital. Unable to undergo surgery there, the patient eventually had the procedure at a private hospital.
"I do not have the financial means to undergo surgery at a private hospital," he said.
Like Kamal, other patients with heart conditions are struggling to access complex eye surgery because of the absence of ICU facilities at the specialised hospital.
Although the hospital offers a wide range of surgical services, it lacks an ICU. Doctors said some patients require general anaesthesia and close monitoring after surgery, making intensive care support necessary in certain cases. Without such facilities, they have to be referred to other hospitals.
Patients said transferring to another hospital means going through fresh registration, securing a new appointment and undergoing additional tests. This delays treatment and increases the financial and emotional burden on patients and their families.
Doctors, however, said not all eye surgeries require ICU support. Routine cataract operations can generally be performed without intensive care facilities. However, depending on a patient's physical condition, the type of surgery and the anaesthesia required, some complex procedures may necessitate close monitoring.
Patients with heart conditions, in particular, require additional precautions before and after surgery, they said.
Dr Sayeed Mehboob Ul Qadir, director of the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital, told Dhaka Tribune that the hospital had never had an ICU since its establishment. He recently assumed office and is working to address patients' basic healthcare needs.
"I cannot comment on matters that predate my joining. The hospital provides necessary surgical procedures free of charge. However, fees are charged for certain diagnostic tests in accordance with government regulations," he said.
The director said general anaesthesia was not necessary for every eye surgery involving heart patients. Many procedures could be performed using local anaesthesia or anaesthetic eye drops.
However, some procedures, including retinal surgery and certain eye muscle operations, may require general anaesthesia. Heart patients undergoing such procedures may need ICU support, he said.
Patients with heart conditions who require general anaesthesia for eye surgery are advised to undergo the procedures at other government medical college hospitals equipped with ICU facilities, he added.
Asked about the difficulties patients face in securing appointments at those hospitals, Dr Qadir said patient numbers exceeded available capacity, resulting in long waiting periods.
Regarding plans to establish an ICU, he said: "Setting up an ICU is not something I can do alone. It requires adequate space, manpower and technicians. I will certainly take the initiative if there is an opportunity to establish one through discussions with the Ministry of Health."
The National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital began its journey in 1979 with 100 beds inside the Shaheed Suhrawardy Hospital Complex in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka. In December 2007, it moved to its own premises in Agargaon and began operating as a 250-bed hospital.
It is now one of the country's leading specialised and referral centres for eye care.
According to hospital sources, around 4,000 patients visit its outpatient department every day. They receive various diagnostic and treatment services for a nominal ticket fee of Tk10.
The hospital also accommodates an average of 220 to 250 inpatients daily. Its outpatient and emergency departments together provide services to around 600,000 to 700,000 patients annually.
To cater to this large number of patients, the hospital performs an average of 60 to 80 minor and major surgeries every day, including around 50 to 60 phacoemulsification procedures for cataract treatment.
Overall, approximately 27,000 to 28,000 eye surgeries are performed at the hospital each year.
The hospital currently has 250 beds. To cope with the growing patient load, there are plans to expand the facility into a 10-storey building and increase its capacity to 500 beds, the director said.

item.title: Factory closures, clashes disrupt garment operations in Ashulia, Gazipur
item.description:
Demands for a Tk30,000 monthly minimum wage triggered protests across major garment-producing areas on Saturday, disrupting operations at dozens of factories in Ashulia and Gazipur and leading to clashes between workers and police.
At least 30 factories in Ashulia and 18 to 20 in Kaliakair, Gazipur, declared holidays amid the unrest. Clashes left at least five industrial police personnel and several garment workers injured, while police recovered three crude bomb-like objects from the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Ashulia.
Superintendent of Police of Ashulia Industrial Police-1 Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan confirmed the factory closures at around 1:45pm on Saturday.
Police sources said workers of Naim Knitwear first stopped working inside the factory in the Kathgara area in the morning. They later came out and staged protests, throwing bricks at several nearby factories.
At one stage, workers and police engaged in chases and counter-chases.
During a visit on Saturday afternoon, a tense situation was observed in Nishchintapur, Kathgara, Zirabo and Narsinghpur areas of Ashulia in Savar.
Speaking to workers, it was learnt that employees of Newage Apparels and Newage Garments in Nishchintapur began a work stoppage in the morning, demanding a minimum wage of Tk30,000, an end to blacklisting and a halt to worker layoffs.
Later, workers at Al-Muslim, Continental and AR Jeans in Kathgara, Naim Sweater and FNF Garments in Narsinghpur, and Trouser Line in Zirabo also staged protests.
At noon, garment workers gathered in Nishchintapur. When police attempted to disperse them, clashes involving chases and counter-chases broke out.
Police later fired tear gas, prompting workers to throw bricks at them. At least 5 industrial police personnel were injured, while several garment workers also sustained injuries.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan said the situation remained tense as workers took positions at different locations and could prevent employees at other factories from working.
He said: “The situation is not very good now due to the workers' protests. Workers are taking positions at different locations. They may obstruct workers at other factories from working. We are trying to explain the situation to the workers. So far, at least 30 garment factories have declared holidays. A police member was hit on the head by bricks thrown by protesters and has been admitted to hospital.”
Inspector (Investigation) of Ashulia police station Harun-or-Rashid said: “Since morning, workers have been staging protests and work stoppages in Zirabo, Nishchintapur and Kathgara. However, the situation was brought under control at noon.”
Khairul Mamun, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, said setting the minimum wage at Tk30,000 was a longstanding demand of workers.
He added that workers must not be blacklisted or dismissed arbitrarily.
Khairul Mamun said the labor minister had announced that a wage board would be formed within October, but the process had not started, creating resentment among workers.
He said a meeting at the Ministry of Labor on Friday night decided that the process of forming the minimum wage board would begin by next Sunday. However, the message had not properly reached the workers, prompting continued protests.
A worker at Newage Apparels, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “The prices of everything have increased, but our wages have not. If our wages are not increased, how will we support our families?”
Meanwhile, industrial police recovered 3 crude bomb-like objects from the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Ashulia at noon.
The objects were found in front of a factory belonging to Nassa Group in the Nishchintapur area.
Mohammad Mominul Islam said: “The matter has been reported to the Bangladesh Police's Anti-Terrorism Unit (ATU). They will come to the scene and take further steps.”
Meanwhile, at least 18-20 factories declared holidays following clashes between police and garment workers protesting for wage increases near the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Kaliakair, Gazipur.
Authorities declared holidays at all garment factories along the 13-kilometer stretch from Konabari to Chandra.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amjad Hossain confirmed the information on Saturday afternoon.

item.title: Garment workers block Dhaka-Tangail highway, clash with police
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway again for nearly three hours on Saturday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, triggering clashes with police.
The clashes broke out around 5:30pm on Saturday when police attempted to disperse the protesters. Police fired tear gas and sound grenades, leaving several people injured.
Earlier, workers had blocked the highway from around 2:30pm, triggering severe traffic congestion. To prevent further unrest, authorities declared holidays at least 12 factories in the area.
The blockade brought traffic to a complete standstill on the highway, causing widespread suffering for commuters.
According to police and local sources, workers of Interstop factory began protesting by blocking the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair Upazila around 2:30pm on Saturday. Workers from several other factories later joined the protest.
During the demonstration, the workers placed sacks filled with soil, wood and bamboo on the highway and set them on fire, bringing traffic to a standstill along several kilometres of the road.
The protesting workers said they had been urging factory authorities to increase their wages and benefits over the past few days.
However, as the authorities failed to reach a decision on their demands, the workers became agitated, stopped working and eventually took to the streets.
According to industrial police and workers, demonstrations demanding higher wages have been continuing for the past two weeks in Konabari, Mouchak and several other areas. Although the government has decided to form a new wage board to review workers' salaries, labour unrest has persisted at several factories.
On Saturday, during the lunch break, workers of Interstop factory refused to resume work and took to the Dhaka-Tangail highway. They later blocked the road by placing sacks of waste and debris from nearby areas on it.
Workers of the neighbouring Divine Textile factory subsequently joined the protest, spreading labour unrest among factories from Chandra to Konabari.
In response to the escalating situation, authorities declared holidays at 12 factories in the area.
After receiving reports of the protest, police from the local police station and industrial police rushed to the scene and tried to bring the situation under control by persuading the workers to end their demonstration.
The blockade began around 2:30pm, causing severe inconvenience to passengers and transport workers. At around 5:30pm, tensions escalated into clashes when police attempted to remove the workers from the highway. Police fired tear gas shells to disperse the protesters, who retaliated by throwing bricks and stones at law enforcers, turning the area into a virtual battleground.
The highway blockade also left thousands of passengers and drivers stranded. Police repeatedly urged the workers to clear the road to ease public suffering, but they ignored the appeals and continued their demonstration, setting fires on the highway.
Police also fired sound grenades in an attempt to disperse the protesters and restore normalcy. Clashes between workers and police continued, spreading panic across the area.
Kaliakair Police Station Officer-in-Charge Shahidul Islam said police were trying to calm the workers and bring the situation under control.
"Authorities have declared holidays at 10 to 12 nearby factories. We have arrived at the scene to pacify the workers and are trying to contain the clashes," he said.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Mohammad Amzad Hossain said the situation had remained normal in the morning, but workers from several factories joined the protest in the afternoon.
"The workers had been blocking the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Palli Bidyut area for about an hour. When police tried to remove them, they hurled bricks and stones at law enforcers, triggering clashes. We are trying to bring the situation under control," he said.

item.title: Al-Arafah Islami Bank holds Town Hall Meeting for Dhaka South Zone
item.description:

The bank’s deputy managing directors Md Fazlur Rahman Chowdhury, Md Asaduzzaman Bhuiyan, Md Aminul Islam Bhuiyan, SM Abu Jafar, and Syed Abul Hashem were present at the event.

He placed particular emphasis on the recovery of classified investments and cost reduction as the bank’s key priorities in the current period.

item.title: Home minister: Future political course must reflect people's will
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Saturday said the country's future political course must be shaped in line with the people's aspirations and national will to ensure a sustainable democratic system.
He stressed the need for broad political consensus and dialogue among all stakeholders, including opposition parties, to determine the country's future direction and introduce reforms that would prevent the emergence of authoritarian rule.
He made the remarks at a seminar titled "Constitutional Crisis in Post-Independence Bangladesh and BAKSAL", the first in the "Democratic Journey" seminar series organized by the July Memorial Museum in Dhaka.
He said constitutional reforms should reflect the aspirations of the July mass uprising and the expectations of the younger generation, with a focus on establishing institutional checks and balances to ensure that no individual or government could exercise unchecked power.
The minister said one of the government's key goals is to establish effective watchdog institutions to protect democracy.
These include ensuring judicial independence, maintaining an impartial Election Commission, introducing a permanent legal framework for a caretaker government system and safeguarding press freedom.
The seminar was chaired by Ehsan Mahmud, director general of the July Memorial Museum, while former interim government Law Adviser Asif Nazrul delivered the keynote speech.
Firoz Ahmed, a former member of the Constitution Reform Commission, and Supreme Court lawyer Habibur Rahman also took part in the discussion.
Salahuddin said that although the Constitution had laid down clear provisions for running the state after independence, the introduction of a one-party system through BAKSAL in 1975 had paved the way for a constitutional crisis and authoritarian rule.
He said the abolition of the caretaker government system through the 15th Amendment in 2011 was a major factor behind the erosion of democracy and the rise of fascist forces in the post-BAKSAL period.
This political course eventually led to the July 2024 mass uprising, when students and people from different walks of life united to bring down the authoritarian regime, he added.
The minister said the country's future political system must reflect the will of the people.
On judicial reforms, he said independence of the judiciary alone was not enough; accountability was also necessary to ensure that no institution of the state could exercise unchecked power.
He also stressed the need for dialogue and political consensus among all stakeholders, including opposition parties, on various reform proposals, including the introduction of an upper house, proportional representation in elections and the holding of referendums.
The minister said the government had no intention of pursuing political vendettas or creating divisions.
He called for unity among political parties and people, saying broad political consensus, guided by the spirit of the July mass uprising and the aspirations of the younger generation, was essential to building a democratic and prosperous Bangladesh.

item.title: Milon calls for climate-resilient, sustainable agriculture
item.description:
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister AKM Ehsanul Hoque Milon Saturday stressed the need to build a sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural system to tackle the challenges ahead.
Milon made the remarks while addressing the inaugural session of the 25th Conference of the Bangladesh Society of Agronomy as chief guest at the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council auditorium in the capital.
"We have made remarkable progress in agricultural production. But the challenge ahead is not just about boosting output; we must keep pace with limited resources, climate change and rapidly evolving technologies," the minister said.
He said efforts must focus on ensuring higher yields from the same land at lower costs, with better quality and environmental sustainability.
Noting that scientists and researchers publish numerous papers and develop new technologies every year, the minister said the reach of such innovations must be measured by how many farmers actually benefit from them.
"Our agricultural universities must not remain mere degree-awarding institutions. They need to emerge stronger as hubs of innovation, problem-solving and transformation of the agriculture sector," he added.
Milon also underscored the need for a skilled workforce for a modern agricultural economy, particularly in operating farm machinery, irrigation technology and food processing.
He said Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) can play a vital role in building these skills.

item.title: Bangladeshi tech entrepreneur Juman Khan's organization now working globally
item.description:
Entrepreneur Juman Khan, co-founder of International Technology of Bangladesh (ITB), is leading the company’s growing presence in the international digital services market, with the organization now working with clients from different countries around the world.
Khan co-founded International Technology of Bangladesh on April 9 last year with the vision of providing professional digital and social media services to clients both in Bangladesh and internationally.
Since its establishment, ITB has expanded its services to include digital marketing, web design, app development, search engine optimization (SEO), Facebook marketing, Instagram marketing, and other social media solutions.
Under the leadership and guidance of Juman Khan, the company has built a growing international client base.
Its clients include well-known individuals and professionals from different sectors, including actors, actresses, sports personalities, singers, administrative officials, members of parliament, and ministers.
At present, around 38 employees are working at International Technology of Bangladesh, with monthly earnings ranging from approximately Tk20,000 to Tk50,000.
According to a company official, ITB currently handles more projects for international clients than for clients in Bangladesh.
“More than 70% of our work is carried out for clients outside Bangladesh. We believe our international work also contributes to the country’s economy. We have reached this position because of the proper guidance and leadership of Juman Khan, the founder and CEO of our organization,” the official said.
The official also said that Juman Khan has created opportunities for students to work alongside their studies, allowing many of them to gain professional experience while also supporting their families financially.
An ITB client from the Philippines also praised the company’s services and the leadership of Juman Khan.
“Working with International Technology of Bangladesh has helped my business move significantly forward in the Philippines. I have worked with many organizations before, but I have never received this level of service. Their marketing work is performing very well, and the quality of their services is excellent. They take every assignment seriously and complete the work professionally, often ahead of schedule,” the client said.
Speaking about his philosophy toward work, Juman Khan, co-founder and CEO of International Technology of Bangladesh, said: “We take every client’s work very seriously, whether the work is small or large. I believe every job should be given equal importance. If you have respect and passion for your work, you can achieve great things even through small tasks.”
With Juman Khan at the helm, International Technology of Bangladesh is continuing to expand its international operations while creating employment opportunities for young people in Bangladesh.
The company aims to further strengthen its position in the global digital services market and showcase the skills and capabilities of Bangladeshi digital professionals to clients around the world.

item.title: Nitai Roy: Bangladesh’s cultural heritage to be promoted in 51 countries
item.description:
The government has planned to showcase Bangladesh's thousand-year-old cultural heritage to the world through cultural diplomacy with 51 countries, Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury said on Saturday.
The government is working continuously to promote the country's arts and culture since the declaration of Nazrul Year, he said.
The minister made the remarks while exchanging views with cultural activists at a meeting organised by Chuadanga Zila Parishad at the conference room of Chuadanga Circuit House.
Initiatives have also been taken to introduce the younger generation to arts and culture through various programmes at educational institutions across the country, he added.
Nitai Roy Chowdhury said Bangladesh has a rich cultural heritage spanning thousands of years, and the government is placing special emphasis on cultural diplomacy to introduce the country's arts, traditions and heritage to people in other countries.
He also announced that Baul festivals would be organised across the country from now on. Traditional folk music, Bhatiyali songs and boat races have been included in the ministry's cultural heritage initiatives, he said.
The government has also taken steps to revive and promote traditional rural games such as Dariabandha, Ha-du-du, Kabaddi and Lathi Khela, the minister added. He said the Prime Minister had been providing immense encouragement for the development of the country's cultural sector.
Cultural activists from Chuadanga raised various demands concerning the development of the district's cultural sector, expansion of artistic activities and promotion of local cultural organisations.
They later submitted a memorandum to the minister outlining their demands for the overall development of culture in the district.
Presided over by Chuadanga Zila Parishad Administrator and District unit BNP General Secretary Sharifuzzaman Sharif, the meeting was attended by local cultural activists and representatives of different organisations.

item.title: Minister: Strong agricultural economy key to national economic growth
item.description:
Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid on Saturday said the country’s economic strength depends on strengthening its agricultural economy, as most people in Bangladesh are directly or indirectly involved in the sector.
“The government believes that a strong agricultural economy will lead to a strong national economy,” he said, adding that modern technology was essential to reducing post-harvest losses and expanding agricultural exports.
The minister was speaking at the inauguration of the country’s first large-scale Gamma Irradiation Centre at the Bangladesh Institute of Nuclear Agriculture (BINA) Regional Research Centre in Bhabanipur of Gazipur.
He said the government was working to reduce dependence on imported agricultural products, particularly onions, and expressed hope that Bangladesh would no longer need to import onions in the future.
The 500,000-curie-capacity facility will use gamma irradiation technology to eliminate harmful microorganisms, prevent spoilage, and extend the shelf life of agricultural products, including onions, potatoes, mangoes, jackfruits, pineapples, and vegetables.
The minister said Bangladesh produced high-quality mangoes and other fruits, but their limited shelf life and difficulties meeting international safety standards had restricted export opportunities.
He said the new technology would help make agricultural products safer and more suitable for international markets, including Australia, China, Pakistan and Europe, where demand for Bangladeshi fruits was growing.
“Bangladesh is an agriculture-based country, yet agricultural products have not become one of its leading export items. Technological limitations are among the main reasons,” he said.
Rashid stressed that the centre's success would depend not only on investment and machinery but also on efficient management and skilled personnel. He said the government planned to establish similar facilities across the country to ensure better market access and fair prices for farmers.
Highlighting food safety, he said the government was also testing the quality of imported food products and would take steps to stop imports of items considered harmful to public health.
According to BINA, China's state-owned China Isotope and Radiation Corporation received the contract to build the centre through an international tender in 2024.

item.title: NBR mandates registration for ‘Startup Sandbox’ facilities
item.description:
Registration with the National Revenue Board (NBR) has been made mandatory for startup companies seeking to avail of Startup Sandbox facilities.
If the NBR fails to decide on a registration application within 60 days of receipt, the application will automatically be deemed approved.
However, the authority reserves the right to cancel registrations if false information is provided or if access to digital systems is obstructed.
The NBR disclosed this information on Thursday (October 29). The provisions were clarified in an order signed by NBR Chairman Ahsan Habib on Wednesday.
This directive was issued to ensure the proper application, effective implementation, and tax compliance of the "Startup Sandbox" provisions outlined in Part II of the Eighth Schedule of the Income Tax Act, 2023.
Under the guidelines, startups intending to access sandbox benefits must meet statutory conditions and register with the NBR by submitting an application addressed to the NBR Member (Tax Appeals and Exemptions).
Applications must be accompanied by:
Upon reviewing the application, the NBR will issue a "Startup Sandbox Registration Certificate" within 60 days.
If no decision is communicated within this window, the application will automatically be considered approved.
The directive also outlines specific procedures for registration cancellation.
If a startup is found to have submitted incorrect information or restricted access to its digital systems, a show-cause notice will be issued, allowing the business 60 days to respond.
Additionally, the startup's representative must be given a reasonable hearing before any cancellation order is finalized.
Registration can only be canceled through a written order detailing valid grounds following the hearing.
Industry insiders note that the Startup Sandbox is a specialized regulatory and policy framework designed by the government for innovative ventures.
Its primary objective is to help early-stage businesses scale smoothly without facing immediate, heavy tax burdens and regulatory hurdles.

item.title: What delaying LDC graduation means for Bangladesh
item.description:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has officially granted Bangladesh a three-year preparatory extension, shifting its Least Developed Country (LDC) graduation deadline from November 24, 2026, to November 24, 2029.
While this reprieve shields the economy from immediate trade shocks, macroeconomic analysts—including former World Bank Dhaka office lead economist Dr Zahid Hussain—caution that this extension must serve as an active window for structural transformation rather than a deferral of tough decisions.
In the immediate term, the deferment is a positive development for macroeconomic stability.
Bangladesh currently benefits from duty-free, quota-free (DFQF) market access for roughly 73 percent of its total exports across 38 major trading partners and international blocs.
Without this extension, graduation would have exposed domestic merchandise exporters to an average tariff burden of 12.50% overnight.
Given that the economy is navigating lingering post-shock vulnerabilities, foreign exchange pressures, and a domestic political transition, the extra three years prevent a jarring contraction in export earnings when external buffers are thin.
In the long run, viewing this extension purely as a comfort zone is dangerous. Bangladesh has effectively been on a graduation pathway since first meeting all three UN criteria (GNI per capita, Human Assets Index, and Economic Vulnerability Index) in 2018.
Having already secured a two-year Covid-19-related extension, the country has had nearly eight years to execute structural reforms.
As Dr Zahid Hussain notes, extending the timeline risks lowering the sense of urgency, fostering complacency, and allowing structural reform inertia to persist. If the breathing room is treated merely as an excuse to kick economic restructuring down the road, the economy will face an even harsher cliff when November 2029 arrives.

item.title: DBA seeks tax exemption on capital gains until 2030
item.description:
The DSE Brokers Association of Bangladesh (DBA) has proposed a full tax exemption on capital gains earned by individual and foreign investors from listed securities until 2030 to restore investor confidence, increase market liquidity and encourage long-term investment in the country's capital market.
The association submitted the proposal to Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, Prime Minister's Special Assistant for Investment and Capital Market Tanvir Shahriar Gani, Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) Chairman Masud Khan and National Board of Revenue (NBR) Chairman Ahsan Habib on Wednesday.
According to the DBA, individual investors currently enjoy tax exemption on capital gains of up to Tk50 lakh from listed securities, while gains exceeding the threshold are generally subject to a 15% tax.
The association has proposed reinstating full tax exemption for individual investors and reconsidering the existing tax regime applicable to foreign individual and institutional investors.
The DBA believes that such incentives would help increase stock market transactions, encourage investors to reinvest their earnings and promote the productive use of domestic savings.
It would also expand equity financing opportunities for listed companies.
Under the proposal, the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act, 2023, should be amended to exempt capital gains from eligible transactions executed through stock exchanges and settled through the designated central depository system.
However, the DBA has recommended retaining the existing tax regime applicable to sponsors, directors and institutional investors.
The association also pointed out that the introduction of a full-fledged Central Counterparty Bangladesh Limited (CCBL) would make capital gains calculation and tax assessment easier.
Considering this, the DBA has sought the tax exemption until CCBL becomes fully operational, saying the measure would provide investors with a more favourable tax environment during the transition period.
DBA President Saiful Islam said an investment-friendly tax regime for individual and foreign investors would help restore confidence in the capital market and encourage long-term investment.
It would also broaden financing opportunities for listed companies and facilitate the government's plans for developing the country's capital market, he added.

item.title: Pedestrian killed, 30 Jamaat activists injured in Satkhira road crash
item.description:
A pedestrian was killed and at least 30 Jamaat-e-Islami activists were injured after a bus carrying them struck the man and plunged into a roadside ditch in Patkelghata, Satkhira.
The accident occurred around 8:30pm on Saturday in the Charabotola area of the Khulna-Satkhira highway, as the activists were returning from a road march organised by the 11-party alliance in Khulna.
The deceased, Abdul Khalek Mollah, 65, was the son of Aftab Mollah of Kashiadanga village in Patkelghata.
Ripon Molla, a neighbour of the deceased, said the bus was returning to Satkhira after the Jamaat activists attended the road march in Khulna. As Abdul Khalek was crossing the road near Charabotola intersection, the bus ran him over, killing him on the spot.
The bus then plunged into a roadside ditch, injuring several passengers. Ripon said the deceased had some mental health issues.
Satkhira Jamaat Secretary General Azizur Rahman said the elderly man suddenly came in front of the bus as it was returning from the road march.
"While trying to save him, the bus carrying our leaders and activists veered off the road and plunged into a roadside ditch, injuring at least 30 activists. The elderly man also died." he said.
Officer-in-Charge of Patkelghata Police Station Toffazzel Hossain said the pedestrian was killed after being hit by the bus carrying Jamaat activists.
He said several passengers were also injured when the bus fell into the ditch. The driver was in critical condition, while the others sustained minor injuries.

item.title: Three bomb-like objects found amid Ashulia garment worker protests
item.description:
Industrial police recovered three bomb-like objects in Ashulia on Saturday amid garment workers’ protests that left more than 10 industrial police personnel and several others injured.
The objects were recovered around noon in front of New Age factory in the Nishchintapur area along the Baipail-Abdullahpur road.
Additional Superintendent of Police of Industrial Police-1 Syed Faisal Islam confirmed the recovery, saying the objects were found during the protests. Police could not immediately determine who had brought or left them at the scene.
Ashulia police station has been informed, and police are expected to take legal action, he said.
Protests began early Saturday when workers from several garment factories in Kathgora Bazar, Nayapara and Nishchintapur stopped work and came out of their factories after 8am.
By noon, workers had gathered on the Abdullahpur-Baipail road in Nishchintapur, where the demonstrations escalated into clashes and vandalism.
Workers from Continental, AR Jeans and other factories allegedly threw bricks and stones and damaged property, including windows at AR Jeans and Continental.
Police and other law enforcement agencies fired tear gas and sound grenades to disperse the protesters and restore order on the highway.
The ensuing clashes left more than 10 industrial police personnel, several workers and pedestrians injured.
The authorities concerned and AR Jeans management declared general holidays amid the unrest.
Industrial Police-1 Superintendent Mohammad Mominul Islam said the situation was under control.
At least 26 factories, including AR Jeans, Continental, Naim Knitwear, New Age, Knit Asia and Sterling Creations, remained closed amid the protests.

item.title: 20 injured in clash over TikTok comment in Brahmanbaria
item.description:
At least 20 people were injured in a series of clashes between two groups in Ashuganj upazila of Brahmanbaria on Saturday, following a dispute over a negative comment on a TikTok video.
The clashes broke out at Ashuganj Bazar in the afternoon, turning the busy marketplace into a battleground and forcing shopkeepers to close their businesses.
According to police and eyewitnesses, tension arose on Friday after a comment on a TikTok video triggered a dispute between two groups from Abir Hati and Nagor Bari areas of Sohagpur village. The dispute initially led to a physical altercation between two young men.
In an attempt to resolve the matter, a mediation meeting was held at Jaru Mia's warehouse in Ashuganj Bazar on Saturday morning in the presence of police and local leaders. Although the two sides reached a settlement, fresh violence erupted around noon after police left the venue.
Members of the rival groups, armed with locally made weapons, engaged in successive clashes, leaving at least 20 people injured. Panic spread across the market as shoppers and pedestrians fled for safety.
Police later rushed to the scene and brought the situation under control after several attempts.
Ashuganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge Md Anisur Rahman said the dispute over the TikTok comment had led to a physical altercation between two youths on Friday.
He said the matter was settled at a mediation meeting in the presence of police on Saturday morning, but the two groups clashed again after officers left.
Additional police personnel have been deployed at Ashuganj Bazar to prevent further violence, he added.

item.title: Garment workers clash with police at Mirpur-10
item.description:
Garment workers clashed with police in the Mirpur 10 area of the capital.

The clashes began at around 11:15 am today, Sunday, and ended at around 11:45 am. Workers had been protesting since morning by blocking the road at Mirpur 10 intersection, demanding that their minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000.

According to eyewitnesses, police repeatedly asked the workers to clear the road. At one point, around 11:15 am, workers threw bricks and stones at the police. The police then began baton-charging them and chased them away. They also used water cannons, sound grenades and tear gas shells.

Garment workers block Mirpur-10 again, demanding Tk 30,000 minimum wage, metro station gates closed

The workers were dispersed as a result. They later regrouped and continued throwing bricks and stones at police from different directions. Clashes and chases between the two sides followed. The situation continued until around 11:45 am.

Garment workers had been protesting since morning by blocking the road at Mirpur 10 intersection in the capital, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000.

At around 8:00 am today, Sunday, workers from several garment factories blocked the road. This has disrupted traffic in the surrounding area.The gates of Mirpur 10 metro station were closed due to the blockade.

Gazipur garment workers block Dhaka–Tangail Highway, set police box on fire

Shortly before 11:00 am, Prothom Alo’s Administration Department official ABM Khairul Kabir, who was at the scene, said he had been unable to enter the station because its gates were closed. He later went to Kazipara station and boarded a metro train there.

Saiful Islam, a sub-inspector (SI) at Mirpur Police Station, told Prothom Alo that garment workers had gathered from several locations in Mirpur this morning and blocked Mirpur 10 intersection. Police have been sent to the scene, he said.

Garment workers had also blocked roads in Mirpur on Saturday over the same demand. The blockade brought traffic to a standstill in Mirpur 10, 11 and 12, as well as surrounding areas, from 10:30 am to 1:00 pm.

Workers clash with police repeatedly in Gazipur, 30 injured 15 vehicles vandalised

At one point, the workers gathered in the Shah Ali area of Mirpur 1. Several markets and garment factories were vandalised there.

There were also scuffles, chases and clashes between the workers and security personnel. In addition, workers threw bricks and stones at a garment factory in the Kalshi area.

Meanwhile, a wage board will be formed today to determine new wages for garment workers. Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said this.

At a press briefing after a meeting at the Department of Labour headquarters in Bijoynagar area of the capital, on Saturday, the minister said there was no reason for workers to continue their protests in these circumstances.

item.title: Many entrepreneurs unable to get loans they need
item.description:
Hat Bakso, a small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) that manufactures souvenirs, applied to a private bank for a Tk 2 million cash credit (CC) loan to finance its business operations.

However, the bank is unwilling to lend more than Tk 400,000–500,000. Bank officials have assured the company that if it provides collateral, they can offer a loan worth up to 70–80 per cent of the value of its assets. Yet, just two and a half years ago, the company had received loans of the amount it needed from two banks and has been regularly paying interest on those loans.

Shafat Kadir, chief executive officer (CEO) of Hat Bakso, told Prothom Alo: “We are new entrepreneurs and do not have assets. However, we maintain regular daily transactions and pay the instalments on our existing loans on time. Even so, the bank is willing to provide only one-fourth of the amount we applied for. We cannot do anything with such a small amount. We also applied for a supply chain loan at another bank but have not received it in three months. How can we expand our business if we cannot get loans when we need them?”

Like Shafat Kadir, many businesspeople are unable to secure the loans they need from banks. Even large businesses are showing little interest in investment. Despite various government initiatives, closed industrial units have not resumed operations on any significant scale. As a result, the sluggish conditions that have gripped the private sector for several years are becoming even more pronounced.

Meanwhile, more than half of the country’s banks have largely withdrawn from industrial lending. Their boards of directors are unwilling to take on any new risks. Consequently, private sector credit growth has fallen to its lowest level in history. Credit growth in the private sector has remained below 5 per cent for six consecutive months. Yet, even with an average lending rate of 10 per cent, credit growth would normally be expected to be at a similar level.

In May, Bangladesh Bank announced a Tk 620 billion incentive package to revive activity in the financial sector. Of this amount, Tk 200 billion was allocated to reopening closed factories.

As of 15 October, Tk 5.61 billion had been disbursed from the fund earmarked for reopening closed factories. Meanwhile, approximately Tk 119.6 billion had been released from the entire Tk 620 billion package by the same date.

According to central bank data, private sector credit growth stood at 4.72 per cent in March. It remained at a similar level in April. In May, it edged up slightly to 4.98 per cent before declining again in June and July.

Credit growth stood at 4.75 per cent in August. As a result, private sector credit growth has remained below 5 per cent for six consecutive months. In the 2025–26 fiscal year, credit growth was 4.47 per cent.

Bank officials say businesses that have already invested are now facing uncertainty, leaving little momentum for new investment. Very little lending is going to the industrial sector.

A large share of the loans being disbursed is being used to finance imports of consumer goods and raw materials. Some consumer loans are also being issued. To increase credit growth, the private sector must regain momentum.

That would lead to an increase in lending. In the past, many loans were disbursed under fictitious names and were not put to much use in investment. This has contributed to the deterioration of the banking sector.

Businesses unable to secure loans

Members of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), including NH Apparels, Munshi Attires, DK Knitwear and Fatullah Fashion, have applied for loans from the incentive fund to reopen 78 closed factories.

Another 109 partially closed factories have also sought loans from the fund. However, the owners of these factories are not receiving much response.

On the matter, BKMEA President Mohammad Hatem told Prothom Alo: “As far as we know, no company in the knitwear sector has received a loan from the incentive fund so far. The boards of a few banks have approved loans for two to four partially operational factories, and the proposals have been sent to the central bank. However, no bank board has approved a loan for any closed factory.”

He added that the government wants to restore momentum to business and trade, and the central bank is sincere in its efforts. However, commercial banks are not coming forward adequately in this regard.

Hifs Agro Food Industries, based in Chattogram, applied to a private bank for a Tk 200 million cash credit loan. The bank offered to lend Tk 30–40 million. However, as that amount would not meet its needs, the company has shown little interest in pursuing the loan.

Syed Md Shoaib Hasan, CEO of Hifs Agro Food Industries, told Prothom Alo that no bank was currently willing to lend more than 70–80 per cent of the value of collateral. In the past, however, banks had provided loans worth 120 per cent or more of the collateral’s value.

“Our products used to take 45 days to reach various countries in the Middle East. Now it takes three months. As a result, we need more working capital than before. But we are not getting support from banks. Consequently, we are losing business opportunities,” he said.

Two companies under the steel-sector RRM Group have an approved credit limit of Tk 6 billion for their business operations. However, the group has sought an additional Tk 2 billion in credit facilities because of the rise in the dollar’s price, the reduction in letters of credit (LC) limits and an increase in other business costs. The bank is not approving the request.

Confirming the matter, RRM Group Chairman and Bangladesh Steel Manufacturers Association Secretary General Sumon Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that 48 companies control 90 per cent of the steel market. Of these, 30–32 companies have failed to secure requests for additional credit limits. Due to a shortage of funds, the companies are operating at half their production capacity. “If this continues, the industrial sector will not be able to recover,” he said.

Credit growth in the past

Private sector credit growth stood at 25.84 per cent in the 2010–11 fiscal year, before falling to 19.72 per cent in the following fiscal year. In the 2023–24 and 2024–25 fiscal years, credit growth was 9.84 per cent and 6.49 per cent, respectively.

An analysis of Bangladesh Bank data shows that credit growth accelerated before and after the national elections in 2014 and 2018.

New initiatives to revive the private sector

The government has taken new policy measures, alongside incentives, to increase the flow of credit to the private sector. To this end, Bangladesh Bank has reduced its policy rate for the first time in 21 months. The repo rate, or policy interest rate, has been lowered from 10 per cent to 9.5 per cent.

As a result, banks’ cost of borrowing from Bangladesh Bank has fallen somewhat, creating scope for lending rates to gradually decline. Relevant stakeholders believe, lower lending rates would help boost investment and employment.

However, entrepreneurs consider infrastructure-related issues, including gas and electricity supply, to be major obstacles. They also take the law and order situation into account. Long-standing problems such as tax policy, bribery and corruption remain as well.

Mohammad Ali, managing director of Pubali Bank, told Prothom Alo that many banks had reduced their lending activities after running into difficulties. Besides, there has been little new investment. However, he expects credit growth to gradually increase as disbursement under the incentive package gets underway.

Will the economy regain momentum?

On the one hand, Bangladesh Bank has taken steps to lower interest rates to stimulate the economy. On the other, it has lifted the lending limit imposed on state-owned Sonali Bank to increase loan disbursements. As a result, the bank will be able to lend as it sees fit in response to customer applications.

Since taking office, the BNP government has placed the highest priority on increasing investment and employment. In its election manifesto, the BNP set a target of turning Bangladesh into a trillion-dollar economy by 2034.

Reducing interest rates was also part of the discussion on investment-friendly policies to achieve this goal. Many sound entrepreneurs are now getting loans at interest rates below 10 per cent.

Abul Kasem Khan, former president of the Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry and vice-chairman of A K Khan & Company, told Prothom Alo that the government measures to stimulate the economy were positive.

Many reforms had been undertaken, and more were underway, to improve the business environment. However, their impact would take time to materialise. The global situation was also not favourable, and business confidence had yet to recover.

Abul Kasem Khan added: “The business environment in Bangladesh has still not improved. It takes a year just to complete the procedures required to start a business. A task that should take one day ends up taking a year. Meanwhile, countries such as China and Thailand have moved far ahead. In this age of artificial intelligence, we need to rethink how to improve the business environment. We are encouraging solar power, but offering no incentives. Many countries are providing incentives for the use of solar power.”

item.title: Tenants leave government colonies as inspections set to begin
item.description:
“On 22 October, the landlord suddenly served me with a notice to vacate the flat. I was at my village home for the Durga Puja holidays at the time. When I returned to Dhaka on the 26th, I could not stay in the flat for even another day. I wandered from place to place, staying wherever I could. The landlord strictly instructed me to remove all my belongings and leave by 31 October.”

A third-year student at Eden Mohila College was describing her experience. She rented a room in a flat in a building at Azimpur Government Colony (Zone B) in the capital. She was one of many students living in the colony as subtenants.

The student was found at Azimpur Government Colony on Saturday at around 11:15 am. She was loading furniture and other belongings onto a van.

Requesting anonymity, the student said the agreement was that the landlord would give at least two months’ notice before asking her to leave.

Similarly, tenants were required to give two months’ notice if they wished to vacate the flat. However, neither condition was respected. Instead, she was forced to leave abruptly.

“We have our final examinations next December. I do not know how I will prepare for them in this situation. It will take me at least a month to recover from this trauma,” she said.

Students from various educational institutions, including the University of Dhaka, Eden Mohila College, Begum Badrunnesa Government Women's College, College of Applied Human Science (Home Economics College) and Dhaka College, rent rooms as subtenants at Azimpur Government Colony. Most of them are female students, who feel safe living in the government colony.

The students rent accommodation there out of necessity, as they come from different districts and securing a place in their respective institutions' halls of residence is not easy. The exact number of students living in the colony is unknown. However, students estimate that the figure could exceed 1,000.

Many government employees rent out their allotted flats. Some let out their entire flats, while others rent out one or two rooms.

Sources say a section of those who rent out their entire flats do so to live elsewhere at a lower cost while earning additional income from their government accommodation.

Another section has substantial additional income and no interest in living in their old government flats. They also want to earn extra money by renting out the properties. Those who rent out one or two rooms mainly do so because their salaries are insufficient to cover their living expenses.

This practice of renting out government accommodation has continued for years in Azimpur and other government colonies across Dhaka.

On Thursday, the Directorate of Government Accommodation, under the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, issued an urgent public notice stating that if any subtenant or tenant remained in a government flat after 31 October, the allotment of the flat to the relevant government employee would be cancelled. The notice also warned of disciplinary and legal action against those concerned.

A significant number of government employees at Azimpur Government Colony used to rent out their flats, while another section disapproved of the practice. Senior-ranking government officials, in particular, were opposed to it.

Speaking about the removal of tenants, Mahbub Alam, general secretary of the management committee of building no. 22 at Azimpur Government Colony (Zone B), told Prothom Alo that some residents might have rented out individual rooms, and complaints had been received about such cases.

“However, everyone has already been asked to leave. There are no tenants left,” he said.

Students said that, over the past few days, hundreds of students and tenants from other professions had been forced to leave their rented accommodation in the government colonies in Azimpur and Palashi.

However, many had yet to find new accommodation, as the search for a new home usually needs to begin at least a month in advance.

A third-year student at Begum Badrunnesa Government Women's College said, “I searched for accommodation in different areas every day until 11:00 pm or midnight. Even then, I could not find anywhere.”

She added, “We are renting accommodation in different places only because we could not secure a place in the halls of residence.”

The student urged the college authorities to arrange accommodation in the residential halls on an emergency basis in view of the situation.

A different picture in Paikpara, Tolarbag

The situation was different at the government officers' and employees' residential area in Paikpara, Mirpur-1. No one was seen leaving their accommodation during a visit to the area from 12:30 pm to 2:30 pm on Saturday.

Conversations with security guards at the colony gate and shopkeepers in the surrounding area yielded the same information. They also said they had not seen anyone leave their accommodation that day.

Meanwhile, several young men were seen in front of the old five-storey buildings at the Walk-up Government Employees' Residential Area in Mirpur-1.

They said the Public Works Department (PWD) had conducted raids on vacant flats and sealed them. Many residents of the area had already moved into the new multi-storey buildings nearby.

Inspections to be conducted

There are government colonies in various parts of the capital. According to statistics from the Directorate of Government Accommodation, the capital has a total of 19,091 government flats of different categories. Demand for rented accommodation is particularly high in the Azimpur area, which has 3,252 flats.

Meanwhile, Jahirul Islam Khan, director of the Directorate of Government Accommodation, told Prothom Alo that tenants and subtenants had been instructed to vacate their accommodation by 31 October.

Officials from the directorate would now conduct inspections. If they found anyone living in a flat as a subtenant or tenant, they would take legal action against the government employee in whose name the flat had been allotted.

Jahirul Islam said most tenants had already left their accommodation, while some were in the process of moving out.

He also said the authorities had not given tenants just one day's notice to vacate their flats. They had been given a week. Moreover, he questioned why people living there illegally should be given additional time, as they were occupying the accommodation unlawfully.

Students said everyone knew that people rented out flats at Azimpur Government Colony. They had no objection to the authorities asking tenants to leave. However, they said there was no need to subject people to unnecessary hardship.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, a student said it was impossible to find accommodation within seven days. She had walked around helplessly searching for a place to stay but had found nothing.

“We are citizens of this country too. We have not committed any serious offence. What harm would it have caused the government if it had given us a month to find new accommodation and move out?” she said.

item.title: Gazipur garment workers block Dhaka–Tangail Highway, set police box on fire
item.description:
Garment workers have staged fresh protests in different areas of Gazipur, demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to Tk 30,000. Traffic on the Dhaka–Tangail Highway has been halted since Sunday morning due to the workers’ protests and blockades.

A police box in Konabari has been set on fire. Five platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel have been deployed to keep the situation under control.

Workers took to the streets and began protesting this morning in Safipur Bazar, Chandra Palli Bidyut, Mouchak and Telichala areas of Kaliakair upazila in Gazipur. They chanted various slogans demanding higher wages.

Garment workers block Mirpur-10 again, demanding Tk 30,000 minimum wage, metro station gates closed

Kaliakair Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Shahidul Islam said workers had been occupying the highway since this morning. As a result, traffic on the highway has come to a halt.

Gazipur Deputy Commissioner Md Nurul Karim Bhuiyan said five platoons of BGB personnel had been deployed in view of the current situation. The number of BGB personnel would be increased further if necessary, he added.

According to factory workers and police sources, garment workers have been protesting in different areas of Gazipur for nearly two weeks, demanding higher wages.

On Saturday, workers blocked the highway at Chandra Palli Bidyut and near Gate 3 of the Ansar Academy in Kaliakair until 8:30 pm. Police later dispersed them by charging batons and firing tear gas shells. Traffic on the highway returned to normal after about five hours.

This morning, workers from several factories, including Korani Knit Composite and Knit Asia in Ratanpur, Kaliakair, and nearby areas, did not report for work and took up positions on the highway in Safipur Bazar.

They began protesting after marking their attendance at the factories. Several nearby factories have declared holidays because of the workers’ movement.

Workers clash with police repeatedly in Gazipur, 30 injured 15 vehicles vandalised

Hundreds of workers later took up positions at various points along the highway, carrying sticks and poles. This brought traffic on the Dhaka–Tangail Highway to a complete standstill, leaving passengers travelling along the route in severe distress.

In the Konabari area of Gazipur city, protesting workers set fire to a police box located in the middle of the highway. They also took equipment and other belongings out of the police box and set those on fire, said Konabari Police Station OC Iftekhar Hossain.

item.title: HSC results re-scrutiny: Applications open, here’s how to apply
item.description:
The results of the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations were published yesterday, Saturday. Nearly 600,000 students have failed.

Many students may not have received the results they expected. Those who wish to do so can apply for re-scrutiny of their results.

The Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee has also announced details of the application process and fee payment rules. Applications must be submitted online. No manual applications will be accepted.

Students dissatisfied with their published results can apply for re-scrutiny from today, Sunday (1 November 2026). The application process will continue until 7 November.

HSC: Exam dates for students who failed 1 or 2 subjects to be announced by 3 November

How to Apply for Result Re-scrutiny

Students must apply online through the designated website to have their results re-scrutinised. They need to visit the website and enter their roll and registration numbers in the designated fields. They must then select their education board from the dropdown list and click the ‘Submit’ button.

Students must then provide their mobile phone numbers. An SMS will be sent to those numbers when the re-scrutiny results are published.

The next screen will display the student’s subject-wise results. To request re-scrutiny of the results in one or more subjects, students must select the relevant subjects and click the ‘Pay Fee’ button.

The fee is Tk 150 per paper. For subjects with two papers, students must apply for both papers. The amount payable will be displayed in the next step. Fees can be paid through bKash, Nagad, DBBL Rocket, Upay and Sonali services. Detailed payment instructions can be found by clicking the ‘Pay’ button on the relevant portal.

More than half of male HSC candidates fail, female failure rate 43.69pc

After paying the fee, students must log in to the application portal and click the ‘Submit’ button. If they wish to add more subjects after submitting an application with a fee payment, they can do so by following the same procedure. However, they will not need to provide their mobile phone number again.

If students need to change or modify their applications before paying the fee, they can click the ‘Delete’ button to withdraw the selected subjects for which fees have not yet been paid. They can then select new subjects. However, once the fee has been paid, the subjects included in the application cannot be withdrawn. Under no circumstances will the fee be refunded.
